evidence:
Plan A: $40 base + $0.10 per GB
Plan B: $15 base + $0.25 per GB
scenarios.hint: Set the two cost expressions equal to each other and solve for the usage — what does the intersection point tell you about which plan wins on each side?
scenarios.prompt: At what monthly usage do the two plans cost exactly the same?
scenarios.situation: Your team is choosing between two cloud-storage pricing plans for a data pipeline. The bill depends on how many gigabytes you store each month.
scenarios.title: The storage-plan crossover
scenarios.why: Set 40 + 0.10g = 15 + 0.25g. Subtracting gives 25 = 0.15g, so g = 166.67 GB — about 167 GB. Below that Plan B is cheaper; above it Plan A wins. Break-even problems are just linear equations in disguise.

evidence:
t=0h: 500 req/s (baseline)
Traffic doubles every 3 hours
Capacity: 32,000 req/s
scenarios.hint: Write the load as 500 times a power of 2, then ask: what power of 2 turns 500 into 32,000?
scenarios.prompt: Roughly how many hours from now will the server exceed its capacity?
scenarios.situation: Overnight traffic to your API is doubling every 3 hours. Right now it is 500 requests per second, and the server's hard capacity is 32,000 requests per second.
scenarios.title: The doubling traffic spike
scenarios.why: Load follows 500 · 2^(t/3). Setting it equal to 32,000 gives 2^(t/3) = 64 = 2^6, so t/3 = 6 and t = 18 hours. Exponential growth looks harmless until the doublings stack up — that is why capacity planning works in powers of two.

evidence: P(x) = -x**2 + 24*x - 80  # profit in $k, x in hundreds of units
scenarios.hint: Break-even means profit equals zero — so you are really being asked for the roots of a quadratic. What factors to 80 with a sum of 24?
scenarios.prompt: At which production levels does the line break even (profit = $0)?
scenarios.situation: A manufacturing model predicts profit (in thousands of dollars) from producing x hundred units: P(x) = −x² + 24x − 80.
scenarios.title: The break-even parabola
scenarios.why: Set −x² + 24x − 80 = 0, or x² − 24x + 80 = 0. Factoring: (x − 4)(x − 20) = 0, so x = 4 or x = 20 — i.e., 400 or 2,000 units. Between those roots the parabola is positive, so profit is positive only in that window.

evidence:
f = lambda x: 2*x + 3
g = lambda x: x**2 - 1
result = f(g(2))
scenarios.hint: Work from the inside out: evaluate the inner function first, then feed its result into the outer one.
scenarios.prompt: What is the value of result?
scenarios.situation: A data pipeline chains two transformations: g(x) = x² − 1 feeds into f(x) = 2x + 3. An engineer runs f(g(2)) and gets a surprising number.
scenarios.title: The chained transform
scenarios.why: First g(2) = 2² − 1 = 3, then f(3) = 2(3) + 3 = 9. Composition is inside-out; the common mistake is evaluating f(2) = 7 and then g(7) = 48, or adding the functions instead of nesting them.

scenarios.hint: Plug a power ratio of 2 into the formula — what is log10(2), roughly?
scenarios.prompt: If the amplifier doubles the signal power, what is the gain in decibels?
scenarios.situation: A radio engineer measures an amplifier stage: output power is exactly twice the input power. Gains are quoted in decibels, defined as 10 · log₁₀(P_out / P_in).
scenarios.title: The doubling decibel
scenarios.why: Gain = 10 · log₁₀(2) ≈ 10 · 0.301 = 3.01 dB, about 3 dB. This is the famous rule of thumb: +3 dB means double the power, −3 dB means half. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, which is why engineers love them.

scenarios.hint: The absolute value measures distance from 50 — how far in each direction is still allowed?
scenarios.prompt: Which latency range satisfies the SLA?
scenarios.situation: Your service-level agreement requires response latency t to satisfy |t − 50| ≤ 15 milliseconds.
scenarios.title: The SLA inequality
scenarios.why: |t − 50| ≤ 15 means t is within 15 ms of 50 in either direction: 50 − 15 ≤ t ≤ 50 + 15, i.e., 35–65 ms. Absolute-value inequalities describe tolerance bands — the bread and butter of SLA and spec writing.

evidence:
4-character temporary codes
Position 1: letter (A-Z, 26 options)
Positions 2-4: letter or digit (36 options each)
scenarios.hint: Count the choices for each position independently, then combine them — do you add or multiply independent choices?
scenarios.prompt: How many distinct temporary codes are possible?
scenarios.situation: Your auth service issues 4-character temporary codes: the first character must be a letter (26 options), and each of the other three can be a letter or a digit (36 options each).
scenarios.title: The code-space count
scenarios.why: By the multiplication principle: 26 · 36 · 36 · 36 = 26 · 46,656 = 1,213,056. Independent choices multiply. This is the same reasoning behind password-strength estimates — each added position multiplies the search space.

evidence: 367 employees enrolled in the birthday-calendar program (366 possible dates, incl. Feb 29)
scenarios.hint: If every date were taken by exactly one person, how many people would that cover — and what does one more person force?
scenarios.prompt: What is the smallest enrollment that guarantees two employees share a birthday?
scenarios.situation: HR wants a guarantee — not a probability — that at least two employees in the program share a birthday. There are 366 possible dates including February 29.
scenarios.title: The birthday guarantee
scenarios.why: The pigeonhole principle: with 366 boxes (dates) and 367 items (people), at least one box holds two. So 367 guarantees a shared birthday. Note 366 does not suffice — one person per date is still possible.

evidence: 10 nodes; sum of all node degrees = 34
scenarios.hint: There is a classic theorem relating the sum of degrees to the number of edges — every edge contributes how much to that sum?
scenarios.prompt: How many links (edges) does the network have?
scenarios.situation: A monitoring tool reports a 10-node mesh network where the node degrees sum to 34.
scenarios.title: The handshake count
scenarios.why: The handshaking lemma: the sum of degrees equals twice the number of edges, since each edge touches two nodes. So edges = 34 / 2 = 17. A degree sum can never be odd — that is a quick sanity check on any topology report.

evidence:
T(1) = 1; T(2) = 1
T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2)  # tasks spawned at depth n
scenarios.hint: Build the sequence term by term — each term is just the sum of the two before it.
scenarios.prompt: How many tasks spawn at depth 7?
scenarios.situation: A recursive job spawns subtasks following T(1) = 1, T(2) = 1, T(n) = T(n−1) + T(n−2).
scenarios.title: The recursive fan-out
scenarios.why: Unrolling: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 — so T(7) = 13. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, and it is a warning: naive recursion here explodes exponentially, which is why real schedulers memoize or iterate.

choices: The disk is not full OR the memory is not full
The disk is not full AND the memory is not full
The disk is full OR the memory is full
The alert logic is a contradiction and never fires
scenarios.hint: Negating an AND flips it to an OR and negates each side — what is the formal name of that rule?
scenarios.prompt: Which condition is logically equivalent to the paging rule?
scenarios.situation: An on-call alert pages when NOT (disk_full AND memory_full). A teammate rewrites it and you need to verify the rewrite is equivalent.
scenarios.title: The negated alert
scenarios.why: By De Morgan's law, NOT (A AND B) is equivalent to (NOT A) OR (NOT B): the alert fires when the disk is not full or the memory is not full. So it pages in every state except both-full — probably not what the author intended, which is exactly why this law matters in review.

evidence: Batch job starts at 10:00, repeats every 7 hours
scenarios.hint: The 100th run is 99 intervals after the start — reduce the total elapsed hours modulo 24.
scenarios.prompt: At what time of day does the 100th run start?
scenarios.situation: A batch job first runs at 10:00 and repeats every 7 hours. You need the wall-clock time of its 100th run.
scenarios.title: The 100th batch run
scenarios.why: 99 intervals × 7 hours = 693 hours later. 693 mod 24 = 21 (since 24 × 28 = 672), so the run starts 21 hours after 10:00 — at 07:00 the next day. Modular arithmetic is the math of anything cyclic: clocks, rotations, hash buckets.

choices: The mean, because it uses every data point
The median, because a single outlier distorts the mean
The mode, because it is the most common value
Report only the maximum; averages hide problems
scenarios.hint: Compute both the mean and the median of those five numbers — which one would a customer recognize as 'typical'?
scenarios.prompt: Which single number better represents the typical response time?
scenarios.situation: Five API response times (ms): 12, 13, 14, 15, 200. One request hit a cold cache. Your status page needs one representative number.
scenarios.title: The lying average
scenarios.why: The mean is (12+13+14+15+200)/5 = 50.8 ms, dragged up by one outlier; the median is 14 ms, which matches four of the five requests. For skewed data the median resists outliers while the mean does not — that is why latency is usually reported as p50/p99, not as a mean.

evidence: mean = 100 ms, sd = 15 ms, roughly normal
scenarios.hint: The empirical rule assigns about 68%, 95%, and 99.7% to one, two, and three standard deviations — which band matches 'about 95%'?
scenarios.prompt: About 95% of requests should fall in which latency band?
scenarios.situation: Request latency is roughly normal with mean 100 ms and standard deviation 15 ms.
scenarios.title: The two-sigma band
scenarios.why: The empirical (68-95-99.7) rule: about 95% of a normal distribution lies within two standard deviations of the mean — 100 ± 2(15) = 70–130 ms. SREs use this constantly to sanity-check whether an 'anomaly' is actually anomalous.

evidence:
Service A uptime: 90%
Service B uptime: 80%
Failures are independent
scenarios.hint: For independent events you combine probabilities with multiplication, not addition — what is 0.9 times 0.8?
scenarios.prompt: What is the probability both services are up at a random moment?
scenarios.situation: Your checkout depends on two services with independent failures: A is up 90% of the time, B 80%.
scenarios.title: The joint uptime
scenarios.why: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72. The common error is adding (1.7, impossible) or averaging (0.85). Series dependencies multiply — which is why each extra dependency drags total reliability down fast.

evidence:
1% of logins are account takeovers
Catches 99% of takeovers; flags 1% of legitimate logins
scenarios.hint: Imagine 10,000 logins: how many takeovers get flagged, and how many legitimate logins get flagged? Compare the two piles.
scenarios.prompt: A login is flagged. What is the probability it is actually a takeover?
scenarios.situation: 1% of logins are account takeovers. Your detector catches 99% of takeovers but also flags 1% of legitimate logins.
scenarios.title: The base-rate alarm
scenarios.why: Out of 10,000 logins: 100 takeovers → ~99 flagged; 9,900 legitimate → ~99 flagged. So about half of all flags are real: 99/(99+99) = 50%. Even an excellent detector drowns in false positives when the base rate is tiny — the single most important lesson in alerting and fraud detection.

choices: Selection bias — the sample does not represent all users
Response bias — users lied on the survey
Confounding — sample size confounds the result
evidence:
n = 2,000 responses
Sent only to users who filed a support ticket last quarter
scenarios.hint: Who was allowed into the sample, and who was left out? A big sample of the wrong population is still the wrong population.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with generalizing this survey to all users?
scenarios.situation: A satisfaction survey got 2,000 responses — but it was sent only to users who filed a support ticket last quarter. Leadership wants to quote the score for the whole user base.
scenarios.title: The ticket-holder survey
scenarios.why: This is selection bias: the sample over-represents frustrated users, so the score cannot generalize. No sample size fixes a biased sampling frame — 2,000 ticket-filers are still ticket-filers. Always ask who was excluded before trusting a number.

choices: No — a shared seasonal cause likely drives both
Yes — the correlation is strong enough to act on
Yes — correlation at r = 0.8 proves causation
No — the sample of one summer is too small to conclude anything
evidence: r = 0.82 between ice-cream sales and drowning incidents (one summer)
scenarios.hint: Ask what third factor rises in summer and could drive both series — correlation needs a mechanism before it becomes causation.
scenarios.prompt: Should the city restrict ice-cream sales to reduce drownings?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard shows ice-cream sales and drowning incidents correlated at r = 0.82 over one summer.
scenarios.title: The ice-cream paradox
scenarios.why: Hot weather drives both: more ice cream sold and more swimming. Correlation never implies causation by itself — look for confounders, mechanisms, and experiments before acting. Dashboards full of correlated metrics are where this mistake scales fastest.

scenarios.hint: Each entry of the product is a dot product of a row of A with a column of B — compute the top-left entry first as a check.
scenarios.prompt: What is C?
scenarios.situation: A graphics pipeline composes two 2×2 transforms by multiplying their matrices.
scenarios.title: The composed transform
scenarios.why: C[i][j] is row i of A dotted with column j of B: C = [[1·2+2·1, 1·0+2·2], [3·2+4·1, 3·0+4·2]] = [[4, 4], [10, 8]]. Order matters (AB ≠ BA), and shapes must line up: (2×2)(2×2) works, (2×2)(3×2) would not.

scenarios.hint: Multiply matching components and add — watch the sign on the middle term.
scenarios.prompt: What is u · v?
scenarios.situation: A recommendation engine scores item similarity with dot products of embedding vectors.
scenarios.title: The similarity score
scenarios.why: u · v = 3(2) + (−1)(4) + 2(1) = 6 − 4 + 2 = 4. The dot product measures alignment: positive means the vectors point roughly the same way, zero means perpendicular. Nearly all modern similarity search is dot products at scale.

scenarios.hint: Solve the simpler equation for one variable first, then substitute into the other.
scenarios.prompt: How many units of each workload can the cluster run?
scenarios.situation: A cluster planner solves for two workload counts: 2x + 3y = 12 (CPU cores) and x − y = 1 (memory ratio).
scenarios.title: The cluster planner
scenarios.why: From x − y = 1, x = y + 1. Substituting: 2(y+1) + 3y = 12 → 5y = 10 → y = 2, x = 3. Check: 2(3)+3(2) = 12 ✓. Solving linear systems is the engine under capacity planning, circuit analysis, and least-squares fitting.

choices: It keeps its direction and is only scaled
It is rotated by exactly 90 degrees
It is reflected across the x-axis
evidence: v is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix with eigenvalue 3.2
scenarios.hint: The defining equation is Av = λv — the output is a scalar multiple of the input. What does a scalar multiple do to a vector's direction?
scenarios.prompt: What does the transform do to v?
scenarios.situation: In a PCA step, v is an eigenvector of the covariance matrix with eigenvalue 3.2.
scenarios.title: The stretched direction
scenarios.why: By definition Av = λv: the transform scales v by 3.2 without changing its direction. Eigenvectors are the 'natural axes' of a transform — PCA keeps the high-eigenvalue directions because they carry the most variance.

scenarios.hint: Rank counts independent rows (or columns) — is the second row really new information, or a copy of the first?
scenarios.prompt: What is the rank of M?
scenarios.situation: A data matrix M = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] feeds a regression. You check its rank before inverting anything.
scenarios.title: The redundant row
scenarios.why: Row 2 is exactly 2 × row 1, so the rows are linearly dependent — only one independent direction exists, rank 1. Rank deficiency is why naive matrix inversion blows up: the matrix has no true inverse, and the regression needs regularization or feature pruning.

evidence:
Transform: scale x by 2, y by 3
Point p = (1, 1)
scenarios.hint: A diagonal scaling matrix multiplies each coordinate by its own factor — apply them independently.
scenarios.prompt: Where does the point p = (1, 1) land?
scenarios.situation: A layout engine scales x-coordinates by 2 and y-coordinates by 3.
scenarios.title: The stretched point
scenarios.why: The transform is the diagonal matrix diag(2, 3), so (1, 1) → (2·1, 3·1) = (2, 3). Diagonal matrices are the simplest transforms: each axis scales independently, which is all a 'resize' operation ever is.

scenarios.hint: Differentiate term by term — the derivative of 3x² is 6x — then plug in x = 2.
scenarios.prompt: What is the marginal cost at x = 2?
scenarios.situation: A cost curve is f(x) = 3x² − 5x + 7. The team needs the marginal cost (the derivative) at x = 2.
scenarios.title: The marginal cost
scenarios.why: f′(x) = 6x − 5, so f′(2) = 12 − 5 = 7. The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change — in economics it is marginal cost, in physics it is velocity, in ML it is the gradient that training follows downhill.

evidence: 100 m of fencing; fence three sides, barn forms the fourth? No — all four sides fenced.
scenarios.hint: If one side is x, the other is 50 − x; maximize the product. Where does a downward parabola peak?
scenarios.prompt: What is the largest area the pen can enclose?
scenarios.situation: You have 100 m of fencing to build a rectangular pen (all four sides).
scenarios.title: The maximum pen
scenarios.why: With sides x and 50 − x, area A = x(50 − x) = 50x − x². A′ = 50 − 2x = 0 gives x = 25, a square, and A = 625 m². Optimization is everywhere in tech: maximize throughput, minimize latency — set the derivative to zero and check it is a max.

scenarios.hint: Distance is the area under the velocity curve — integrate 2t from 0 to 3, or sketch the triangle.
scenarios.prompt: How far does the robot travel in the first 3 seconds?
scenarios.situation: A robot's velocity is v(t) = 2t m/s for the first 3 seconds.
scenarios.title: The area under velocity
scenarios.why: Distance = ∫₀³ 2t dt = [t²]₀³ = 9 m. Integration accumulates a rate into a total — velocity into distance, request rate into total requests, marginal cost into total cost. The area-under-the-curve picture never lies.

scenarios.hint: The chain rule says: derivative of the outside (at the inside) times the derivative of the inside — what is the derivative of 2x + 1?
scenarios.prompt: What is h′(1)?
scenarios.situation: A composed model is h(x) = (2x + 1)³. Backpropagation needs h′(1).
scenarios.title: The chained derivative
scenarios.why: h′(x) = 3(2x+1)² · 2 = 6(2x+1)², so h′(1) = 6 · 9 = 54. The chain rule is the entire mathematical basis of backpropagation: every layer's gradient is the product of the layers outside it. Forgetting the inner derivative (the ×2) is the classic error.

scenarios.hint: Factor the numerator — does anything cancel with the denominator before you take the limit?
scenarios.prompt: What is lim(x→2) f(x)?
scenarios.situation: A dashboard formula f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) is undefined at x = 2, but values nearby suggest it approaches something.
scenarios.title: The hole in the graph
scenarios.why: Factor: (x−2)(x+2)/(x−2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2, so the limit is 4. The function has a removable discontinuity — a 'hole' — at x = 2. Limits let you reason about the value a formula is heading toward even where it is not defined.

scenarios.hint: How many half-lives does it take to go from 100 g to 25 g? Multiply by the hours per half-life.
scenarios.prompt: How long until only 25 g remain?
scenarios.situation: A 100 g sample decays with a half-life of 4 hours.
scenarios.title: The decaying sample
scenarios.why: 100 → 50 g is one half-life, 50 → 25 g is two. Two half-lives × 4 h = 8 hours. Exponential decay runs caches (TTL), radioactive dating, and drug dosing — anywhere a quantity loses a fixed fraction per unit time.

scenarios.hint: Percent change is (new − old) / old — what is the increase relative to the original $240?
scenarios.prompt: What is the percent increase?
scenarios.situation: A vendor raises your plan from $240/month to $300/month.
scenarios.title: The price hike
scenarios.why: (300 − 240)/240 = 60/240 = 0.25 = 25%. The denominator is always the original value — using the new $300 as the base (giving 20%) is the standard mistake, and vendors count on it.

scenarios.hint: Each year multiply by 1.05 — apply it three times. How is that different from 5% × 3 = 15% simple interest?
scenarios.prompt: What is the balance after 3 years?
scenarios.situation: You park $1,000 in an account earning 5% annual interest, compounded yearly, for 3 years.
scenarios.title: The compounding dollar
scenarios.why: 1000 × 1.05³ = 1000 × 1.157625 = $1,157.63. Compounding earns interest on interest, beating the $1,150 simple-interest figure. The gap looks small over 3 years and enormous over 30 — that is the whole story of investing.

scenarios.hint: Weight each outcome by its probability and add — wins positive, losses negative.
scenarios.prompt: What is the expected value of one play?
scenarios.situation: A carnival game: 60% chance to win $50, 40% chance to lose $100.
scenarios.title: The carnival bet
scenarios.why: EV = 0.6(50) + 0.4(−100) = 30 − 40 = −$10. A negative expectation means you lose $10 per play on average — the house edge, quantified. Expected value is the rational way to price risk, from insurance to feature bets.

scenarios.hint: Multiply each score by its weight as a decimal, then add — the final counts more than double the midterm.
scenarios.prompt: What is the course grade?
scenarios.situation: A course grades the midterm at 30% (you scored 80) and the final at 70% (you scored 90).
scenarios.title: The weighted grade
scenarios.why: 0.3(80) + 0.7(90) = 24 + 63 = 87. Weighted averages run GPA, portfolio returns, and blended metrics — anywhere components matter unequally. The plain average of 85 would underweight the final.

scenarios.hint: There are 8 bits in a byte — convert megabits to megabytes first, then scale up to a minute.
scenarios.prompt: How many megabytes can you download per minute?
scenarios.situation: Your connection is 10 Mbps — megabits, not megabytes, per second.
scenarios.title: The bits-to-bytes trap
scenarios.why: 10 Mb/s ÷ 8 = 1.25 MB/s; × 60 s = 75 MB/min. The bit/byte confusion is the oldest trick in ISP marketing. Dimensional analysis — carrying units through every step — catches it every time.

scenarios.hint: Multiply 3 cm by 50,000, then convert centimeters to kilometers in stages.
scenarios.prompt: What is the real-world distance?
scenarios.situation: A site map at 1:50,000 scale shows 3 cm between two data-center sites.
scenarios.title: The map scale
scenarios.why: 3 × 50,000 = 150,000 cm = 1,500 m = 1.5 km. Scale factors are pure ratios — the same math behind map reading, blueprint takeoff, and model-to-production unit conversions.

lessons.title: Algebra & Functions — Core concepts
concepts: Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, which is why engineers love them.
Linear equations: break-even problems are just linear equations in disguise.
Exponential growth looks harmless until the doublings stack up — that is why capacity planning works in powers of two.
Factoring: (x − 4)(x − 20) = 0, so x = 4 or x = 20 — i.e., 400 or 2,000 units.

g = lambda x: x**2 - 1
result = f(g(2))

lessons.title: Technical Math - Core concepts
concepts: Propositional logic is the math of conditionals: truth tables, De Morgan's laws, and implication. Every WHERE clause and if-statement is a proposition - write them so their negations are obvious.
Combinatorics counts before you code: permutations when order matters, combinations when it doesn't. Define the experiment precisely first - most counting errors are definition errors.
Induction proves statements about all n: verify the base case, assume the statement for k, derive it for k+1. It is the template for proving loops and recursion correct.

Linear algebra is the language of machine learning: vectors, matrices, dot products, and matrix multiplication as transformation. Eigendecomposition finds the principal axes of data - the computation inside PCA.
Statistics summarizes honestly: center (mean/median/mode) plus spread (variance) plus shape. A metric without its distribution is a rumor - watch for skew, outliers, and sampling bias.
Graphs model relationships: vertices, edges, paths. BFS and DFS traverse; shortest-path and spanning-tree algorithms solve networks, dependencies, and state spaces.

example.code:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[2.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 2.0]])
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eig(X)
print("variance along each axis:", eigvals)
print("principal axes:\n", eigvecs)
example.walkthrough: Eigendecomposition returns how much variance lies along each principal axis (eigenvalues) and the axes themselves (eigenvectors). PCA keeps the axes with the most variance and drops the rest - this two-line computation is its core.

pitfalls: Common trap: correlation implying causation - control for confounders before claiming a cause.

Common trap: == on floats - compare with a tolerance (math.isclose) instead of exact equality.
Common trap: off-by-one in counting - state whether order matters and whether repetition is allowed before computing.

Optimization is everywhere in tech: maximize throughput, minimize latency — set the derivative to zero and check it is a max.
Principle: the derivative is the instantaneous rate of change — in economics it is marginal cost, in physics it is velocity, in ML it is the gradient that training follows downhill.

10 Mb/s ÷ 8 = 1.25 MB/s; × 60 s = 75 MB/min. The bit/byte confusion is the oldest trick in ISP marketing.
Dot product: the dot product measures alignment: positive means the vectors point roughly the same way, zero means perpendicular.
